questions.q: Per this lesson, who patches both the operating system and SQL Server itself for Azure SQL Database and Azure SQL Managed Instance?
options: Microsoft, for both the OS and SQL Server, on both options — that's what makes them PaaS
You, for both the OS and SQL Server, on both options
Microsoft patches the OS but you patch SQL Server on both options
It varies randomly by subscription tier
questions.explain: Both Azure SQL Database and Managed Instance are PaaS: Microsoft manages OS and SQL Server patching for both.

questions.q: Why does SQL Server on an Azure VM require you to patch both the OS and SQL Server yourself?
options: Because it is IaaS — Microsoft provides only the infrastructure, and everything above it, including the OS and SQL Server, is yours to manage
Because Microsoft does not support automated patching on any Azure option
Because it is actually a PaaS product with unusually limited automation
Because Azure VMs cannot run Windows Update or SQL Server updates at all
questions.explain: SQL Server on an Azure VM is full IaaS, the opposite ownership split from the two PaaS options.

questions.q: This lesson says full IaaS looks 'strictly worse' for patching but is the right call in what situation?
options: When you need OS-level access PaaS won't give you — a third-party agent on the box, an unsupported feature version, or compliance language naming the exact patch level
When you want the fastest possible deployment time with zero management
When you never need to patch anything at all
When your workload has no infrastructure requirements whatsoever
questions.explain: IaaS trades more patching work for real control — OS-level access that PaaS structurally cannot provide.

questions.q: Why are Azure SQL Database and Managed Instance both classified as PaaS despite exposing very different amounts of SQL Server surface?
options: Because 'PaaS' refers to who manages the platform layer (OS and engine patching), not to how much instance-level surface is exposed to the user
Because they are actually identical products with different names
Because Managed Instance is really IaaS despite being labeled PaaS
Because Azure SQL Database exposes more surface than Managed Instance
questions.explain: PaaS isn't one point on a dial — both keep the patching promise, but Managed Instance exposes near-full instance surface while Azure SQL Database hides it almost entirely.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what should drive the choice between the most-PaaS option and a more IaaS-leaning option for a given workload?
options: How much of the platform the workload actually needs to control, versus how much you'd rather Microsoft own so it stops being your on-call problem
Always choosing the cheapest listed price regardless of management overhead
Always choosing IaaS because it offers more features in every case
The alphabetical order of the product names
questions.explain: This is the same decision lever Chapter 3 revisits repeatedly: every layer Microsoft manages is a layer that stops being your responsibility.
